# Vaṭṭakajātaka (Ja 35)

**ID:** Ja 35
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Vaṭṭakajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Quail
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja35
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Vaṭṭakajātaka* (Ja 35), translated as *The Quail*, is a narrative belonging to the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. According to the framing narrative (*paccuppannavatthu*), the Buddha recounted the story while on an alms-pilgrimage through Magadha after an advancing jungle fire was extinguished [SuttaCentral; Galasek 2016]. In the story of the past (*atītavatthu*), the Bodhisatta was born as a young quail [Appleton 2010; War Yar Mein Da 2015]. When a forest fire swept through his nesting grounds, his parents fled, leaving the unfledged bird defenseless [Appleton 2010; Söhnen-Thieme]. Facing the fire, the Bodhisatta performed a solemn "act of truth" (*saccakiriya*) by recalling the perfection of past Buddhas and their Dhamma, proclaiming that he possessed wings that could not yet fly and feet that could not run (*santi pakkhā apatanā santi pādā avañcanā*) [War Yar Mein Da 2015; Söhnen-Thieme]. By the power of this truthful declaration, the fire turned back; the commentary regards this extinguishing of the flame as one of the four eon-lasting wonders (*kappatthiyapāṭihāriya*) where no fire can ignite for the remainder of the cosmic cycle [Appleton 2010; Galasek 2016].

A direct canonical parallel to this tale is found in the *Cariyāpiṭaka* (Cp 29, *Vaṭṭapotakacariya*), and versions also appear in northern Buddhist literature such as Āryaśūra's *Jātakamālā* [SuttaCentral; Söhnen-Thieme]. DharmaNexus records no significant Pali-internal reuse or cross-language matches above the threshold [DharmaNexus]. Outside Buddhist corpora, verbal echoes and narrative adaptation of the quail's verse are preserved in the *Śārṅgakopākhyāna* of the *Mahābhārata* [Söhnen-Thieme]. Because of its association with the power of *saccakiriya* and protective verses (*paritta*), the Bodhisatta quail is popular in Southeast Asian protective traditions, including Thai quail *yantras* [Appleton 2010]. In material culture, the jātaka is attested in Pali epigraphy as well as on inscribed terracotta plaques from early Pagan in Burma [Salomon 1998; Luce et al. 1970].
